# EDUCATOR. ATTORNEY. PUBLIC SERVANT.
# ABOUT ROB
Rob Fuentes is a son of the Central Valley. Born in the heart of Fresno, Rob has dedicated his life to public service in the city that he calls home–fighting to expand opportunities for working families just like his.
Rob is a civil rights attorney in Fresno and the current President of the State Center Community College District (SCCCD) Board of Trustees, where he works with teachers, trades, and businesses to ensure that our Fresno City College students have the skills and experience necessary to succeed in a modern, 21st century economy. Rob also teaches at San Joaquin College of Law, educating the next generation of law practitioners in Fresno and throughout the Valley.
​
Previously, Rob served as an Assistant U.S. Attorney, handling cases involving white-collar fraud, wildfires, and civil rights violations. Earlier in his career, he worked in private practice, representing workers in cases involving wage-and-hour violations, discrimination, and retaliation. Rob also served on the Fresno Planning Commission, where he strove to make it easier and less burdensome to develop housing throughout the city. In addition, he served on the board of California Rural Legal Assistance (CRLA) and volunteered with Kids in Need of Defense (KIND), representing unaccompanied children in their immigration proceedings.
​
The product of a farmworker family, Rob learned from an early age the value of hard work, sacrifice, and perseverance. He was the first in his family to graduate from college, and he holds a BA from Stanford, an MPP from the Harvard Kennedy School, and a JD from Yale Law School.
As a city councilmember for District 1, Rob will be will be dedicated to increasing affordability for our residents, such as by advancing policies and programs that reduce the costs of housing, transportation, and childcare. He will also work with our law enforcement and non-governmental partners to build safer neighborhoods, pursuing holistic measures that enhance accountability while increasing investments in preventive interventions. A committed coalition-builder, Rob will also partner with our business and labor communities to spur economic and community development, ensuring that we attract and retain businesses, create good-paying jobs, repair our roads and sidewalks, and expand our parks and communal spaces throughout District 1.
Rob will work hand in hand with community partners to develop neighborhoods where residents can live, work, play, and thrive--neighborhoods that we are all proud to call home.
​

Priorities
# Where Ariana stands
Strong communities don’t just happen. They are built by neighbors who show up for one another, and they require a government that does the same. Right now our city is at a crossroads: will we keep building outward, or will we prioritize the neighborhoods we call home?
The Crossroads
## What SEDA would cost us
Through the Southeast Development Area (SEDA), elected officials and special interests are rushing a plan to expand our city limits into Southeast Fresno so developers can build new expensive homes. This would stretch police, fire, trash collection, and water services far too thin.
SEDA is profitable for some, but it leaves us with higher service rates, broken streets, struggling parks and schools, abandoned businesses, and dilapidated housing.
“We can’t afford to be a stepping stone for ambitious politicians.”
Many of us are working two or more jobs as utilities and housing costs go up while our income stays the same. We can build thriving parks, more trees, safe routes to school, and homes families can afford, and we don’t have to leave our neighborhood to get it.
How Decisions Get Made
I want you to know where I stand on the issues that matter. My biggest priority is to make public policy decisions alongside residents, so I will host regular neighborhood meetings throughout the district and proactively engage with our schools to make sure I’m hearing directly from you.
No to SEDA
## No to SEDA’s outward expansion
- Protecting our taxpayer dollars from being used to line developers’ pockets
- Protecting essential services like police, fire, trash collection, and water from being stretched too thin
- Protecting our utility rates from continuing to skyrocket
Yes to Safety
## Public safety in our neighborhoods
- Establishing a Residential Response Team for issues like loose dogs and neighborhood theft
- Prohibiting collaboration between ICE and local law enforcement
- Bringing back our City of Fresno Youth Commission
- Addressing illegal dumping and encampments near neighborhoods, businesses, and schools
- Supporting the Better Roads Safe Streets initiative
- Building and fixing more parks, and investing in more community center activities
- Planting more trees in every neighborhood
For Families
## Partnering with our schools
- Investing in Safe Routes to School through accessible sidewalks and traffic calming measures
- Expanding summer enrichment camps to better align with caregivers’ working schedules
- Paid youth internship programs
Affordability
## Housing every family can afford
- Expanding funding and eligibility for the home repair program
- Making rents more affordable and protecting renters from wrongful evictions
- Expanding homeownership assistance programs
- Expanding partnerships for mental health support
- Partnering with key stakeholders for affordable housing alternatives
Make It Happen
## A platform is only as good as the people behind it
Every door knocked, every phone call and every yard sign planted is powered by people who live here.
Get Involved
Want to help? See upcoming volunteer events.

## JOSAN NARIP
Selma has been my home for more than 25 years, this is where my wife and I have built our lives, raised our children, and invested our time and energy into the community we love. We are blessed to have a son in middle school and a daughter in high school, both in SUSD. Sarah Almond 4 Clovis City Council District 5
Issues I Want to Address for You
The biggest challenge that we are currently facing in Clovis is "low-income" versus "affordable" housing. Many people are framing our current, mandated housing requirement as a need for “low income" housing, but what Clovis actually needs is housing that is affordable-affordable for young adults and working families. It has become very difficult for college students and new graduates to afford to live independently. These are young professionals who want to move to or come back home to Clovis. We also need to draw working families to Clovis. That will only happen if we provide affordable housing options. Many families are working very hard to be able to put their children into Clovis schools. The “Clovis Way of Life” should be attainable for anyone who wants to share it.
Many current residents are wary of new development in or next to their existing neighborhoods. That should be respected. New development should enhance existing communities and not interfere with them. Neighborhood safety is paramount when planning for future development and continued positive growth. Understanding increased traffic volume and its effect on the condition and maintenance of our roadways, pedestrian trails and bike routes are essential to the continued safety of our community.
Many Clovis residents have voiced their concern about transportation. Our community wants and deserves safer roads, less traffic congestion, and a more robust, user-friendly public transit system. Measure C has been essential in funding many of the recent projects but is expiring in 2027. The state has stepped in, and the replacement, Measure S, Better Roads, Safe Streets, will be in the hands of the voters this November. We need to use these funds to continue improvements to our streets, public transit system, and trails.
As your City Council District 5 Representative, I will be your ear, your voice, and your workhorse to ensure that Clovis remains a safe, thriving, and desirable place to call home. As a Clovis resident, just like you, I want our community to be a place where everyone is proud to call home.

## Clovis: Our Successes and Our Challenges
Councilmember Drew Bessinger reflects on how far Clovis has come, the road ahead for District 5, and the shared vision that will carry our city into 2050.
Read the Message
Meet Drew
## A lifelong commitment to the community we call home.
Drew Bessinger has spent his career in public service — leading with integrity, listening to residents, and delivering results. From backing our first responders to supporting the small businesses that make our city special, Drew brings the kind of steady, experienced leadership our City Council needs.
He's a proud family man, US Army veteran, a neighbor, and a leader who believes local government should be transparent, accountable, and always focused on the people it serves.
Read Drew's Story
Priorities
## What Drew is fighting for
Real priorities for real families — the issues that shape everyday life in our city.
### Public Safety
Fully support our first responders, keep our neighborhoods safe, and make sure every family feels secure at home and out in public. Clovis is the safest city in the valley, and we need to keep it that way. Equip our Fire Department with all the equipment needed to respond both inside our city limits and when deployed State-wide for wild land fires and other mutual-aid responses, including earthquakes and weather-related disasters. Additionally, ensure that our Public Works staff has the same level of emergency response capability and equipment to deal with major issues like water and sewer line breaks, or being called to assist other cities and counties to deal with major emergencies when needed. Drew knows that when bad things happen, it's too late to play catch-up! The safety of Clovis does not end with our police and fire personnel. Our safety also includes our Public Works staff that ensures that our water is clean, our toilets flush and sewage is treated, and our roads are properly maintained. It's a dance sometimes, but a necessary dance!
### Local Business
Cut red tape for small business, invest in downtown, and grow the local jobs that keep our city thriving.
### Responsible Leadership
Transparent decisions, careful spending, and a City Hall that answers to the residents who live here.
### Quality of Life
Clean parks, streets, and trails enhance our neighborhoods. Making sure that debris and graffiti are removed quickly prevents the reoccurrence of these nuisances.
### Larger Businesses/Health Care Opportunities
We have worked closely with larger businesses too, like Costco (our #1 sales tax producer) and other national retailers to ensure we are competitive with our neighbors and bring the goods and services Clovis wants and needs. In addition, we have worked hard to make Clovis the medical care destination in Central California. We have worked closely with Community Hospitals, Kaiser, St. Agnes, Central Valley Indian Health, United Health Care, and the VA to create Clovis as the destination for health care. The VA recently broke ground on their facility at Armstrong and Herndon, with the hope that other medical offices, with both treatment options and jobs to follow. This will open health care options to our seniors and our parents, our veterans and families, and our families and neighbors to get quality health care right here in Clovis.
### City of Clovis Highlights Over the Last 10 Years
Over the past decade, the City of Clovis has distinguished itself as one of California's premier communities — earning the title of #1 Safest City in the Central Valley for more than a decade, growing the total citywide budget from $179 million to $395.3 million, and increasing the General Fund Emergency Reserve from $11 million to over $28 million. Combined, Police and Fire added approximately 82.5 public safety positions over the past ten years.
Read more
#### Public Safety — Safest City in the Valley
- Clovis has been designated the #1 Safest City in the Central Valley for more than a decade.
- California Crime Index (2022): Clovis CCI = 630 — the lowest in the region.
- Clovis was also named the #1 Best City in California to raise a family, confirmed in multiple years by third parties.
- Police and Fire together consume 87% of the City's discretionary General Fund revenues.
- The City was awarded a $6.0 million Police grant to combat organized retail crime, funding five officers and one police service officer beginning in FY 2023–24.
- Fire Department expanded from 67 total positions (FY 2016–17) to 92.5 adopted positions — a net gain of approximately 25 positions.
- Fire Station 6 opened in the Loma Vista area, the City's first new fire station in over a decade.
- Fire Station 2 was reconstructed in the Helm Ranch Neighborhood.
- Fire Training Facility enhanced with new classrooms.
#### Fiscal Management & Financial Stability
- Emergency Reserve Rebuilt: grew to 20.3% of the 2024–25 general fund budgeted expenditures, up from a great-recession low of 5.5%.
- Structurally Balanced Budget maintained throughout the decade.
- Measure Y passed with over 66% voter approval — a 1% sales and use tax providing significant investments in Police, Fire, parks, streets, and senior services.
- COVID-19 Economic Recovery: unemployment rate peaked at 13% in May 2020 and recovered to approximately 3.8% by March 2023.
- Five-Year Forecast Discipline: consistently published and adhered to a Five-Year Financial Forecast.
- Achieved delay in legislation requiring electrification of heavy-duty vehicles, avoiding significant expenses and service disruptions.
#### Infrastructure & Capital Investment
- Ongoing street reconstruction across Barstow, Bullard, Shaw, Sierra, Sunnyside, Ashlan, Peach, and Willow Avenues, plus ADA improvements citywide.
- Fire Training Facility expanded with additional classrooms constructed in Southwest Clovis.
- Fire Station 2 reconstructed on Minnewawa near Santa Ana Avenues.
- SCADA system upgraded for water and sewer infrastructure controls.
- New North Civic Center complex designed and constructed — including a new Senior Center, Transit Center, and expanded Fresno County Library.
- Water infrastructure investments continued: new wells, expanded recycled water distribution mains, groundwater recharge facilities, and additional water supply secured.
- Loma Vista Village Green constructed and unveiled.
#### Community & Quality of Life
- 97–98% of residents recommend Clovis as a place to live and raise a family across multiple National Citizen Survey cycles.
- Expanded senior services, recreation programs, parks maintenance, and transit services throughout the decade.
- 50 new citywide positions added in FY 2025–26 alone — the largest single-year staffing expansion.
- General Plan Update is now underway, setting the framework for the next 20 years of planned, sustainable growth.
#### Economic Development & Business Growth
- Top ten employers generate 14,199 jobs in Clovis, with over 40,000 jobs total — up from under 30,000 ten years ago.
- Clovis Community Medical Center expansion brought over 1,000 new jobs.
- Veterans Administration Clinic at Armstrong and Herndon began construction.
- California Health Sciences University established its permanent campus in the Research and Technology Park.
- Dry Creek Business Park expanded using redevelopment bonds.
- Centennial Plaza in Old Town Clovis opened two new buildings, increasing activity and event space.
- New Costco on Clovis Ave. opened during the reporting period.
- Shaw Avenue Corridor Study Phase 2 attracted new retail, hotels, and restaurants including Costco, Vallarta, Chick-fil-A, Panda Express, Planet Fitness, At Home, Habit Burger, and Hobby Lobby.
- Cabinet Connection Manufacturing Facility opened in Clovis.
- Loma Vista Marketplace Development brought Tractor Supply, restaurants, Ross, Grocery Outlet, Butterfish & Made-In.
- Fresno County redeveloped a major industrial complex, adding 1,000 jobs to Clovis.
- Industrial vacancy in Clovis averaged just 0.7%, with lease rates nearly doubling over the decade.
By Councilmember Drew Bessinger
### Improving Our Older Neighborhoods
When I moved to Clovis in 1984, my young sons and I lived in an apartment near Letterman Park. Two years later, thanks to my GI Bill, I bought our first home near Gettysburg and Sunnyside. It was small, but it fit our needs. In 1997, I bought a new home and kept the first one as a rental until selling it in 2004. Today I live near Clovis and Alluvial, where I enjoy a great yard, easy access to our trail system, and two beautiful city parks right behind me.
My wife’s parents moved to Clovis in 1961 and bought a home near Helm and Shaw, where my mother‑in‑law still lives. Back then, the neighborhood was filled with long‑term homeowners who knew each other well. My wife, Yvonne, grew up with the freedom to roam the neighborhood with friends. Parks were uncommon in those days—your backyard was your playground.

Meet Drew
# A lifetime of public service.
Proud to serve the City of Clovis, California.
## Drew's Story
Drew Bessinger has spent his entire adult life in service — to his country, to public safety, and to the community of Clovis. From the U.S. Army Military Police, to a career in law enforcement, to City Hall, Drew has always shown up when he was needed.
Drew and his young sons, ages 4 and 2, moved to Clovis in 1984. Drew moved from Santa Barbara, where he was a police officer, so he could raise his kids as a single dad and be able to buy a home. After working for the University Police Department at Fresno State for almost 3 years, Drew transferred to the Clovis Police Department in 1987. Drew's CPD career spanned the next 3 decades as he worked patrol, detectives, youth services, and SWAT as he rose through the ranks to Captain. Drew retired in 2009 with 30 years of civilian law enforcement. Drew then began a succession of interim police chief jobs for 4 cities, and finally as the airport police chief at Fresno Yosemite International Airport. He retired from law enforcement (again) in 2021.
Drew's service to Clovis didn't end with his retirement from Clovis PD. Drew served for 3 years as a personnel commissioner and then ran for the Clovis City Council in 2017. Even though he was out fundraised almost 3-1, Drew knocked on over 2,500 doors to take his message directly to the citizens of Clovis. Drew's efforts garnered a resounding victory with 68% of the vote. Drew served as the Clovis Mayor during the first awful year of the pandemic. Drew lead the charge to protect our citizens and help small businesses that were deemed "non-essential" by Sacramento politicians. Drew has been reelected twice. Drew juggled being a single dad and full time police officer as he attended Fresno State part-time for 10 years. Drew holds an AA in Administration of Justice (1983) from Santa Barbara City College and a BA in Public Administration (1995) from Fresno State. Drew also holds the breadth of California Peace Officer certifications from the Basic Certificate to the Executive Certificate.
Drew has been a steady, common-sense voice for the residents of Clovis. He stands with our police officers and firefighters, champions responsible growth, protects our small business community, and works to keep Clovis one of the safest and most family-friendly cities in California.
Drew has been married for 26 years to Yvonne Avila Bessinger, a proud Clovis HS Class of 76er and a 65 year Clovis resident. Yvonne's family moved to Clovis in 1961, and her mother still lives in the same house in SW Clovis.
Drew and Yvonne are proud residents of Clovis. They love our schools, the rodeo and other Old Town events, and watching Clovis grow and still have that "small-town" feel. I want my grandchildren to inherit the same lifestyle we had. That's the Clovis Drew is fighting to protect — and to hand off even stronger to the next generation.
A Life of Service
## From the US Army, to Law Enforcement, to City Hall
U.S. Army
### Serving as a Military Police Officer
Drew's career of service began in uniform — building the discipline, integrity, and leadership that shaped everything to come. Drew served his nation for 4 years, including almost 3 years in Germany, as a Military Police Investigator with an MP Customs unit. Drew's father was an Army veteran, wounded and captured during the Battle of the Bulge in January 1945. In 2025, Drew honored his dad's service at an event on the day and location of his dad's capture in Belgium. Drew's great-grandfather served in the Union Army during the Civil War. Drew is proud of his family's legacy of service to our nation, and in his service to the citizens of Clovis. Drew served our nation in the uniform of a United States Army Soldier and kept our nation safe and free for his children and subsequent generations.
Law Enforcement
### Police Chief for 5 Cities and Clovis PD Captain
Drew's background makes him a strong advocate for community safety, and for the men and women of our police and fire departments. Drew has served as a law enforcement officer with the Department of Defense, State of California and 7 local governments, five as the Police Chief. Drew sought more responsibility as he rose through the ranks. Drew was often the person sought out for difficult or sensitive problems. From Internal Affairs to auditing the evidence rooms, Drew ensured standards were adhered to. As a Police Chief, Drew took over two agencies in melt-down and made the difficult and controversial decisions necessary. True leadership requires decisive action; Teddy Roosevelt said “In any moment of decision, the best thing you can do is the right thing, the next best thing is the wrong thing, and the worst thing you can do is nothing.” Drew can withstand the arrows when the difficult decision is obvious and ethical.
Clovis Community
### Member of the Clovis City Council since 2017 and Mayor from 2019-2021.
From Old Town parades, events honoring our veterans, or simply getting into his truck to see problems first-hand, Drew and his family are proud to be part of what makes Clovis special. Being in a leadership position isn't always easy. Some decisions will be non-controversial. Some decisions will not be popular but absolutely necessary. It's important to have people who will not be concerned about their next reelection but in making the correct decision for the citizens for all of Clovis. That's one of the advantages of having public servants with no ambition for their next office ... just serving you.
## Experience & Leadership
U.S. Army Military Police veteran
Clovis Police Captain
Chief of Police for five local cities
Nationally published author of several law enforcement related articles
Clovis City Councilmember since 2017 and Mayor 2019-2021
Strong advocate for our police and fire personnel, and ensuring our City services are top notch
Champion of small business and responsible growth
30-year Police Academy Instructor at Fresno City College
42 year Clovis resident, husband, father, grandfather and community leader
## Why I'm running
"I have been in public service a long time. I seek the opportunity to continue to serve the community that I served, where I raised my kids, where I met my bride, and to make sure it's a great place for my grandkids to live. As a retiree, I have the time and the energy to get out there and see what needs to be fixed. I have no asperations for higher office, I want to continue to serve my hometown and it's citizens. I'm running to make sure the next generation of Clovis families gets that same chance — safe streets and schools, strong local businesses, great parks and trails, logically planned growth, and a City Hall that never forgets who it works for."

## About Mike
Born and raised in northwest Fresno, I’ve had the honor of serving our community not just as a resident but as a neighbor, small business owner, and dedicated public servant. As a second-generation small business owner, I learned firsthand the value of hard work, responsible budgeting, and the importance of creating opportunities that uplift families and strengthen our local economy. These lessons have guided my public service and continue to define my approach to leadership.
In 2019, the people of Fresno’s District 2 entrusted me with the privilege of serving on the Fresno City Council — a role I’ve approached with deep commitment and a clear focus on results. In 2025, my peers elected me Council President — one of the highest honors on the council — and in 2026 I was re-elected to serve a second consecutive term, something that had not happened in over 20 years.
### Leadership Through Results
As a Councilmember, I’ve worked tirelessly to deliver meaningful outcomes for our neighborhoods in northwest Fresno and across our city:
### Strengthening Public Safety
I have consistently advocated for fully staffed Police and Fire Departments — ensuring our first responders have the tools, training, and resources necessary to protect our families, homes, and businesses.

Drawing on my experience as a small business owner, I’ve championed fiscally responsible policies that balance the budget, reduce bureaucratic barriers, and help local entrepreneurs thrive. I believe government should empower job creation and not hinder it.

In 2025, I successfully sponsored a series of council actions addressing key community concerns, including ordinances targeting metal theft, investments toward economic development partnerships, and resolutions supporting public health and business programs.
### Infrastructure and Quality of Life
I’ve pushed for synchronized traffic signals, improved safe routes to schools, and completion of critical projects like Veteran’s Boulevard — investments that make our neighborhoods safer and more functional for families.
### Why I’m Running for County Supervisor
Fresno County Supervisor District 1 is home to hundreds of thousands of residents, including the cities of Fresno, Kerman, Mendota, Firebaugh, and the northwest region of Fresno County. I’m running to bring bold, practical leadership to the Board of Supervisors — leadership that reflects our shared values of public safety, economic opportunity, and family-centered community investment.
### Advocate for improved countywide infrastructure and safer roads.
### Support resource investment for law enforcement and fire protection throughout the district.
### Promote smart growth that attracts jobs, improves access to services, and ensures every community — urban and rural — can thrive.

Public service is more than a title — it’s a responsibility to listen, to lead, and to deliver for the people who call this community home. Whether it’s in northwest Fresno, Kerman, Mendota, or Firebaugh, your voices, your concerns, and your aspirations are what drive my work each and every day.

Classify only the literal source evidence, without background political inference.", "candidate": "Des Haus", "race": {"office": "City Council Member", "jurisdiction": "City of Clovis", "district_or_seat": "District 5", "term": "4 years", "election_type": "general"}, "recorded_campaign_url": "https://des4clovis.com/", "source_url": "https://des4clovis.com/", "source_title": "Des Haus for Clovis City Council, District 5 | November 3, 2026", "full_source_text": "Skip to content
DES HAUS · DISTRICT 5 Menu
Clovis · Election Day November 3, 2026
# Des Haus
Clovis City Council — District 5
Clovis First. Clovis Always.
Get involved Am I in District 5?
For the first time in over a century, District 5 elects its own councilmember. Only District 5 votes in this race.
See the District 5 map →
Why now
## District 5 has never had
a voice of its own.
For more than a hundred years, Clovis chose its council citywide. Every neighborhood folded into one ballot, one conversation. It worked. The people who served in those years built the town we all chose to move to, and they have our thanks for it.
This November, that changes. For the first time, District 5 elects its own councilmember — not someone representing all of Clovis who happens to live nearby, but someone answerable to these streets, these intersections, this side of town.
That is a genuinely new job. Nobody has held it before. And the next ten years here are going to be decided by budgets, infrastructure, and growth arriving faster than the roads and water to serve it.
That's the work I've done for a living. Multi-million dollar budgets, large-scale infrastructure, and the kind of complex regulation that costs cities money when nobody at the table understands it. I already watch Clovis tax dollars as Co-Chair of the Measure Y Oversight Committee. I'd like to do it from the dais.
Clovis — Gateway to the Sierras
About Des
## A proven leader. A local neighbor.
More than thirteen years in Clovis. Two daughters in Clovis Unified. Co-Chair of the Measure Y Oversight Committee.
Des Haus is a business leader with a background in the energy and infrastructure sectors, specializing in strategic partnerships and large-scale project management. She has built a career navigating complex regulation and managing multi-million dollar budgets — and she isn't a career politician. She's a practitioner who knows how to drive efficiency and deliver results.
Des was appointed by the City Council to the Measure Y Oversight Committee, and was nominated by her fellow members to serve as its Co-Chair. In that role she reviews how Clovis spends its public safety sales tax — pressing on expenditures, on timing, and on whether the money is actually there when the city says it is. It is unglamorous work, and it is the reason she knows where this budget has slack and where it doesn't.
Des first came to Clovis as a Fresno State student. She left for a while, and then chose it again — this time to settle down and raise a family. More than thirteen years later she's still here, a wife and a CUSD mom with two daughters in local schools. She chose Clovis for the same reasons you did: the safety, the schools, the values. Most people pick a hometown once. Des picked this one twice.
Out in the community, where the work actually happens.
Priorities
## What I hear at the door in District 5
01
### Your tax dollars, watched closely
Money approved for one purpose has a way of drifting toward another once the vote is over. I do this work now as Co-Chair of the Measure Y Oversight Committee, and I'll keep doing it from the dais.
02
### Growth that pays for itself
Clovis is one of the fastest-growing cities in California. New rooftops arrive faster than the roads, water capacity, and staffing that serve them. Development should carry its own infrastructure costs instead of pushing them onto the neighbors who are already here.
03
### Neighborhoods that stay safe
As a mother, public safety isn't abstract to me. Clovis is growing quickly and our police and fire staffing has to grow with it — which means funding those positions properly and making sure the people doing the job have real support behind them. That is a budget question as much as a policing one. I'll push for Measure Y dollars to reach front-line staffing, and for open, honest conversations from the dais with the staff who actually do the work.
Endorsements
## Who's backing Des
Law enforcement, county leadership, and neighbors across District 5.
Proudly endorsed by
Peace Officers Research Association of California
Local & regional leaders
Buddy MendesFresno County Supervisor Luis ChavezFresno County Supervisor Jordan WamhoffMadera County Supervisor
County leaders across California

- Luis AlejoMonterey County
- Chris HowardDel Norte County
- Rex BohnHumboldt County
- Grant CarmonGlenn County
- Tony ArendtGlenn County
County supervisors who have worked with Des on infrastructure, budgets and public projects.
District 5
## Clovis votes by district for the first time
After more than a century of at-large elections, Clovis adopted council districts in 2025. Districts 1, 4, and 5 are on the ballot this November — and only District 5 voters choose this seat.
Not sure which district you're in? Text your address to 559.593.3902 and we'll tell you.
Get involved
## District 5 is about 24,000 people
A few thousand votes decides this seat. Ten conversations with your own neighbors will move this race more than anything else — including money.
### Volunteer
Tell us what you're up for. Someone will follow up personally.
### Contribute
Every dollar in a district race goes further than you'd think.

## MEET DR. ARAMBULA
## Dr. Joaquin Arambula
##### Emergency Room Physician, Dedicated Public Servant, Father of Three
Dr. Joaquin Arambula is the first Latino physician elected to the California Assembly. He has served in the State Assembly since April of 2016. He has proudly represented the 31st Assembly District, which has included over 60 percent of the City of Fresno and rural cities in Fresno County.
​
As an emergency room doctor, he trained in downtown Fresno and worked in a rural hospital in Selma, CA for almost a decade. There, he saw the emotional and financial toll on people struggling with illnesses that access to health care could have prevented. He was determined to improve health care for everyone.
​
Dr. Arambula served as Chair of the Assembly Budget Subcommittee No. 1 on Health and Human Services from 2016 to June 2023. He has focused on improving health care access and affordability and ensuring the protection of safety net programs for working families. He has authored the “Health4All” bills, known as Assembly Bill 4, that have expanded full scope Medi-Cal coverage to all undocumented adults. He also increased access to Medi-Cal for seniors and the disabled.
​
He also is a staunch advocate of efforts to address the critical statewide shortage of doctors and medical providers, specifically in the Central Valley.​​

Classify only the literal source evidence, without background political inference.", "candidate": "Michele Cantwell-Copher", "race": {"office": "County Superintendent of Schools", "jurisdiction": "Fresno County", "district_or_seat": "At large", "term": "4 years", "election_type": "general"}, "recorded_campaign_url": "https://reelectcopher2026.com/", "source_url": "https://reelectcopher2026.com/proven-leadership/", "source_title": "Leadership - Dr. Copher for Fresno County Superintendent of Schools", "full_source_text": "# Testimonials
# Proven Leadership
#### Dr. Michele Copher
Fresno County Superintendent of Schools
In June 2022, I was honored to be elected as your Fresno County Superintendent of Schools with 68% of the vote. My commitment has never wavered: I am deeply devoted to improving the lives of students through the power of education.
Over the past term, I have prioritized fiscal responsibility, achieving $2 million in staffing savings, balancing the CTEC High School budget with a $1.4 million annual saving, and relocating Kids Café to save $350,000 annually — while better supporting our Special Education Adult Transition students. Student achievement is steadily rising across our Fresno County schools, with measurable gains in ELA, Math, English Learner progress, and specific student improvements across all districts. Our schools are earning recognition too: 8 Schools to Watch, 5 California Distinguished Schools, and 5 Golden Bell Awards in just the school year 2024-25. We host over 250 attendees at our annual Safe Schools Summits. Since the Community Schools state granting program began in 2023, more than $175M has been invested in our district and charter schools.
Looking ahead, I am excited to build on this momentum — expanding student success, strengthening safe schools, and enhancing school-community partnerships through Community Schools. With decades of experience and an unwavering commitment to our students, I ask for your continued support. Endorse, share, and vote for proven leadership in June 2026!
January 1, 2026
Dear Friends of Fresno County Education,
As we begin the new calendar year, my third as your Fresno County Superintendent of Schools, I am proud of the collective work being done on behalf of our students. I want to take a moment to share some of the progress and accomplishments we have achieved together. These highlights reflect not only the success of our students, but also the dedication of the adults and community partners who are working tirelessly to ensure their future.
- Schools: Through strong partnerships with law enforcement, parents can be assured that children are both physically and psychologically safe in Fresno County schools. Visitor management systems, cameras, fencing, and coordinated communication with law enforcement enhance campus safety, while Safe School Ambassadors, cyber training, anti-bullying programs, and student monitoring software support social well-being.
- Improved Student Outcomes and Achievement: Over the past three years, Fresno County students have demonstrated steady gains in reading and math. Secondary schools are seeing increased participation in A-G coursework, dual enrollment, and Career Technical Education. Chronic absenteeism has largely returned to pre-pandemic levels, and countless individual student achievements reflect that excellence is thriving across our county.
- Expanded Mental Health Services: In partnership with the Fresno County Department of Behavioral Health, the All for Youth initiative now deploys over 200 clinicians to serve more than 5,000 students annually. In addition, state grants have allowed FCSS to open 13 new Wellness Centers on school campuses.
- Recognition for Excellence: Fresno County schools and districts continue to shine statewide and nationally. In the past three years, our schools have been honored with 5 National Blue Ribbon awards, 10 California Distinguished School awards, 10 Middle Schools to Watch designations, and 10 Golden Bell Awards.
- Increased Community Support: Together, we have secured more than $175 million in state funding to expand vital services such as social supports, food and clothing pantries, and tutoring. All 12 local school bonds placed on ballots last year were approved by voters—a powerful testament to our community’s confidence in public education.
- Cross-Sector Partnerships: FCSS continues to lead the Fresno Cradle to Career network, engaging 15 systems leaders and over 70 partner agencies to improve outcomes for youth ages 0–22 through coordinated health and education services.
- Stronger Relationships with School Leaders: Attendance and engagement at monthly Superintendent Network meetings remain strong, with superintendents collaborating on legislative advocacy, governance in special education, and other shared initiatives.
- Fiscal Responsibility: In my first year as Superintendent, we reduced teacher overages, transitioned Kids Café into a more sustainable in-house Produce Stand, and balanced the CTEC High School budget—achieving more than $5M in savings while rebuilding public trust in our fiscal stewardship.
- Philanthropic Engagement: The Foundation @ FCOE has raised more than $27M to date, supporting programs in early literacy, the arts, and STEM, further enriching opportunities for our students.
- A Clear Sense of Direction: For the first time in many years, our office has a unified vision, reflected in a Strategic Plan, an Annual Report to the Community, and a Pro-Child Legislative Advocacy Plan. These efforts affirm our commitment to transparency and community partnership in raising up our students.
Together, these milestones reflect what is possible when schools, families, and community partners work in unison for the benefit of our children. I remain deeply committed to ensuring every student in Fresno County has the opportunity to learn, thrive, and succeed.
Thank you for your continued support. With your help, we will continue to make Fresno County a place where every child’s future is bright.
Sincerely,
Dr. Michele Cantwell-Copher
Fresno County Superintendent of Schools
## What Happens If We Keep Moving Forward?
### My Vision for the Next Four Years
- Improve literacy
- Expand career pathways
- Strengthen school safety
- Recruit and retain teachers
- Increase student attendance
### Vision
As your Fresno County Superintendent of Schools, my vision for the next four years is simple: every child deserves the opportunity to thrive, and every family deserves a school system that prepares students for a successful future.
Together, we will continue improving the lives of children and families through outstanding teaching and learning, strong partnerships with our communities, and a commitment to student success at every stage of development. We will expand access to high-quality early childhood education, strengthen literacy, mathematics, and STEM achievement, and ensure students have the support they need to reach their full potential.
We will continue increasing A-G course offerings, dual enrollment opportunities, and career technical education programs so that every student graduates with a clear plan for college, career, military service, or other meaningful pathways. By working alongside educators, families, businesses, and community leaders, we will prepare the next generation to enter adulthood ready to contribute, lead, and strengthen the communities they call home.
Our best days are ahead, and together we will create even greater opportunities for every student in Fresno County.

# The Platform
Fresno is too expensive. Singh will lead an affordability agenda to lower costs and make life easier.
## Fighting for An Affordable Fresno
Capping City-Owned Utility Hikes
Fresno families are being crushed by skyrocketing city utility bills, including trash rates, which have risen nearly 80% in just five years. I will fight to cap future rate hikes on trash, require audits before any increase, and make sure residents are never forced to pay for wasteful spending or mismanagement. These essential services must be affordable for working families and our seniors on fixed incomes. Basic services like water, sewer, and trash must be affordable, predictable, and run in the public interest. Corporations and commercial property owners must pay their fair share. For too long large users have avoided penalties and rate increases, while residential customers absorb the impact. Residents must not be asked to shoulder the costs of corporations.
Taking Action on Rising Utility Costs
Families shouldn’t have to choose between heating their homes and paying rent. I’ll push Fresno to reduce gas costs through smarter housing policy, real assistance programs, and protections that keep savings in residents’ pockets. We will push for more expanded senior utility discounts and a community benefit fund to support residents. While the City does not control gas rates (PG&E), I will support policies that work to reduce overall household costs, expand access to assistance programs, and ensure savings flow directly to residents.
Building a Fresno Affordability Agenda and Coalition
Fresno’s cost-of-living crisis won’t be solved by City Hall acting alone. I commit to bringing together residents, labor, small businesses, housing advocates, and community organizations to build a Fresno Affordability Agenda focused on lowering everyday costs, from housing and utilities to transportation and childcare. By uniting voices across the city around practical, people-first solutions, we can turn shared priorities into real policies that make Fresno a more affordable place to live and raise a family.
## Investing in Fresno’s Infrastructure Future
Fixing our Streets and Neighborhoods
Fresno deserves streets and neighborhoods that are safe, accessible, and cared for, no matter the ZIP code. I will prioritize fixing potholes, repairing and upgrading sidewalks, and improving street lighting, while tackling blight and long-neglected infrastructure in our neighborhoods. When our streets are well-maintained and our public spaces are clean and safe, communities are healthier, businesses are stronger, and neighbors feel connected and proud of where they live.
Expand Operation CleanUp
I will work to expand Fresno’s Operation Clean Up program to include apartment residents and mobile home parks, especially where tenants are already paying for sanitation services indirectly through rent and utility pass-through fees but are excluded from receiving the benefit. This expansion will reduce illegal dumping, improve neighborhood cleanliness, and ensure working families and renters have the same access to basic city services as homeowners. Fresno should not make it more expensive to be poor. Clean and safe neighborhoods must be a right for everyone, not a privilege for a few.
Illegal Dumping Hurts Working Families.
We will lead a data-driven crackdown on illegal dumping by combining faster cleanup, targeted enforcement in repeat hotspots, and real accountability for commercial dumpers who treat our neighborhoods like landfills. At the same time, I will expand disposal options, especially for renters, apartment residents, and mobile home parks, so working families aren’t forced to choose between paying high fees or living with trash. Clean streets are a public health issue and a dignity issue, and I will make Fresno a city where every neighborhood gets the same standard of cleanliness, service, and respect.
Shading our Neighborhoods and Expanding Tree Cover
The temperature on a treeless Fresno street can be 15 degrees higher than one with shade. That is the difference between a high utility bill and a crisis. I will introduce a plan to aggressively close the shade gap in the City. We will focus on 'high-heat' zones: our playgrounds, transit stops, and residential blocks to slash local temperatures and put money back in your pocket by reducing the need for home cooling during hot Valley summers.
More Parks and Green Spaces
Fresno needs more parks and green spaces now. I’ll be a community champion to push for strategic land acquisition, stronger development requirements, and real partnerships so we turn Measure P promise into visible parks where our kids can play and families can gather. By investing in our parks, we invest in the well-being and quality of life for all Fresnans.
## Putting Fresno Small Businesses First
Cut Red Tape and Speed Up Permitting
Small businesses are the heartbeat of Fresno. We want our city to be the land of small mom and pops, but too many entrepreneurs are buried in red tape before they ever open their doors. I will fight to ensure we streamline and speed up city permitting with clear timelines, real accountability, and hands-on support so local businesses can open, expand, and hire without months of delays. When we make it easier to start and grow a business, we create jobs, strengthen neighborhoods, and build a Fresno economy that works for all of us.
A "Fresno First" Procurement Policy
The City of Fresno spends millions of dollars every year on everything from office supplies to construction and consulting. Often, these contracts go to large firms outside the Valley. I will work to pass a "Fresno First" ordinance that gives local businesses a stronger bidding preference on city contracts. This ensures that taxpayer dollars don't just leave the city, but instead recirculate through our local economy, supporting Fresno jobs and Fresno families.
Champion a “Vacant to Vibrant” Program
We have far too many boarded-up windows West of 99, on the Shaw Corridor, and in the Tower District. However instead of signs of decay, the City should support our local entrepreneurs to see these as the launchpads for Fresno’s next local legends. A Vacant to Vibrant Program will bridge the gap for neighborhood dreamers, moving entrepreneurs out of their garages, and into the heart of our commercial corridors by subsidizing short-term leases and slashing the red tape that stalls progress. We aren’t just filling empty spaces; we are growing a homegrown economy where every artist, baker, and maker has the tools to thrive and stay right here in the 559.
## Building Affordability & Housing Fresno
Preventing Homelessness by Strengthening Eviction Protection Program
I will champion a new Bridge Grant Fund that gives renters and landlords a fast, common-sense alternative to eviction, providing small support payments of up to $1,500 to resolve small arrears, before a family is pushed into crisis. This fund will be streamlined, transparent, and designed to keep people housed while protecting small landlords from unnecessary losses. And because our goal must be housing stability for our entire community, I will pair it with stronger access to legal counsel, mediation, and support services so more disputes are resolved fairly, quickly, and without displacement.
Prioritizing Mental Health Support
A major issue facing our homeless communities is a lack of access to mental health support. I will lead a council-backed campaign to increase mental health services and supports through our existing structures, and begin the push for the City of Fresno to begin the process of creating its own local, responsive agency dedicated solely to the families of our City.
Reform and Expand Fresno Affordable Housing Trust Fund
We will expand home access by transforming the Affordable Housing Trust Fund by cutting through the red tape that has hindered building. By reforming the fund to prioritize "infill-first" projects and smaller-scale neighborhood developments, we will ensure that city dollars stay within city limits to build the "missing middle" homes our workforce deserves. This is about more than just funding; it is about reclaiming our pro-housing status to unlock millions in state matches and proving that Fresno has the vision and the will to house our entire community.
## Supporting Fresno Schools, Youth, LGBQTIA+, & Immigrants
Creating a D1 Youth Green Ambassador Corps and other opportunities
We will build a 100+ youth strong stipended leadership and workforce development program, D1-FORCE (Fresno Outreach for Resilient Community Environments), aimed at those enrolled at local colleges, universities, or D1 youth residents, especially attending Fresno High, Bullard High, Central East High, and Justin Garza High School. Students will get to work on real-world city projects, from climate-resilient landscaping in our neighborhoods to data-driven tech solutions at City Hall. By creating a direct pipeline between our classrooms and our civic infrastructure, we are ensuring that Fresno’s brightest minds don't just graduate here but they stay, lead, and build their careers right here in Fresno.
Prioritizing Public Schools at the Center of Fresno’s Future
I will champion a future where the City of Fresno stops treating our schools as small silos and starts treating them as the front porch of our neighborhoods. We will build pride in our schools-first approach by making the City a primary investor in the success of our campuses, not just through words, but through concrete infrastructure that ensures every school is the safest, cleanest, and most vibrant part of its zip code. When we invest in the streets, parks, and safety surrounding our schools, we aren't just funding District 1; we are building a city that honors its children as its greatest asset. This will be a new era of partnership between District 1 and the school districts that serve the area, both Fresno and Central Unified.
Establish a REAL sanctuary city policy and support for our LGBQTIA+ and immigrant families
I will lead efforts for Fresno to adopt a real Sanctuary City policy that ends local cooperation with ICE and makes it clear: our city will not help separate families. We will expand free legal support and know-your-rights resources so immigrant residents, especially our LGBTQIA+ communities, can protect themselves from deportation, fraud, and exploitation. Fresno should be a city where everyone feels safe reporting a crime, going to school, and accessing basic services, because strong communities are built on trust, not fear. I will work tirelessly to assure ALL residents feel safe in the City.
## Restoring Trust in Fresno
A People’s Budget: Fresno Dollars, Fresno Priorities
I will bring a People’s Budget to District 1 so residents, not lobbyists or insiders, help decide how city dollars are spent in our neighborhoods. Through regular community assemblies and public voting, District 1 families will set the priorities for investments like street repairs, parks, lighting, youth programs, and other support. This is how we build real trust in government: by putting decision-making power directly in the hands of the people.
Public Safety is Community Safety
Public safety is community safety. When residents feel safe, our neighborhoods thrive, families stay rooted, and small businesses grow. Our Fresno peace officers play a critical role, and I’ll protect what’s working, but police can’t do it alone, because safety goes beyond policing. It also means community working towards crime prevention, compassionate mental health response, opportunities for housing stability, innovative youth opportunity, caring but firm addiction treatment, and neighbors and neighborhoods coming together, so every District 1 community is safer.
Restore Planning for Fresno’s Future
The City of Fresno’s recent decision to cut long-term planning weakens our city’s ability to plan with vision and listen to neighborhoods before major development decisions get made. I will fight to restore a dedicated long-range planning team in the City to create real neighborhood plans and actually implement them. With clear public benchmarks and accountability, we will rebuild trust and ensure Fresno’s future is shaped by the people who live here, not backroom deals. It is time we empower and listen to the professionals and workers that serve our City rather than punish them at the behest of special interests.
Unapologetically Against Corruption
Fresno has a history of far too many examples of politicians putting personal gain over public good, and I’m running as one of the few that is not as a political climber, but rather a Fresno resident with a mission to serve our city with integrity. The ballot is filled with perennial candidates looking for a position; I am a resident on a mission! I will champion strong ethics reforms, transparency in City Hall operations, and enforceable accountability measures so taxpayers know exactly how their dollars are being spent and who they benefit. Restoring trust means putting people over power, ending backroom deals, and building a Fresno government that works for working families, not insiders.
Standing with City Workers
We have many people in the community that wake up every day to serve our City. These are bus drivers, peace officers, firefighters, technical specialists, public safety personnel, administrative staff, frontline service workers, managers, executives, and so many more. Supporting our city workers, especially the dedicated staff at City Hall, is essential to delivering effective, responsive government for Fresno residents. I will advocate for fair compensation, safe working conditions, professional development opportunities, and clear pathways for advancement so that our public servants feel valued and empowered to serve our community with excellence. - Cut unnecessary delays and streamline permitting for starter homes, ADUs, modular housing, and other affordable housing options.
- Invest in water and sewer infrastructure so communities can build the housing working families need.
- Protect renters, seniors, and mobile-home residents from displacement while expanding the overall housing supply.

### Protect Farming, Water & Farm Jobs
- Fight for a reliable water supply for farmers, farmworkers, families, and rural communities.
- Protect agriculture from policies that threaten local farms and jobs and make sure West Fresno County has a strong voice in county and state decisions.
- Support family farms and agricultural businesses by improving infrastructure and cutting unnecessary red tape.
- Prepare the next generation for agriculture by expanding training in ag-tech, water management, equipment, and other modern agricultural careers.

About
# Meet Ariana
Born in Madera to farmworker parents, raised as one of six, and for fifteen years a neighbor organizing alongside other parents in South Fresno.
Dear Neighbor,
Welcome. My family and I are honored to do this work alongside the community. My husband Kevin is a teacher, and for 15 years I have been working alongside other parents in South Fresno, advocating for better parks, safer streets, and affordable housing.
District 7 is the only home my two children have ever known.
My neighbors have told me they simply do not feel safe taking their children to our neighborhood park. I did not see myself running for office, but for too long our district has been used as a political stepping stone while our neighborhoods continue to be left behind. The people in my life have taught me that good things are worth fighting for, especially for those we love.
I was born in Madera to farmworker parents and raised as one of six children. My siblings and I often joined our parents in the fields, helping them achieve their dream of homeownership. Our neighborhood faced its share of vacant homes, underfunded schools, and limited resources, and I still cherish the memories of bike rides and borrowing ingredients from neighbors for my mom’s dinner.
When I was 12, my brother was born with Down syndrome, and I learned quickly that the health of a community often depends on taking the needs of others into account. I volunteered in his classrooms growing up, then became a substitute teacher, intending to eventually teach special education.
After graduating from Fresno State in 2010, Fresno became home. Through my church community I joined local efforts like park cleanups, school staff appreciation events, and civic engagement initiatives. I saw how the struggles of my childhood, housing insecurity, a lack of public spaces, and working multiple jobs, mirrored those of my neighbors. For the last 15 years I have continued to work alongside neighbors advocating for safer streets, better parks, and affordable homes.
My professional career has spanned the classroom, non-profit organizations like Every Neighborhood Partnership, and first-hand experience inside City Hall. As Community Relations Director for Fresno City Council District 3, I tracked infrastructure projects like roads, sidewalks, and park renovations to ensure they were completed on time, helped residents resolve complicated issues, and shaped policies including the Blighted Vacant Building Ordinance and expanded support for small businesses.
That is why Kevin and I see our home as part of a stronger community, built through connection and action, whether we are hosting neighborhood gatherings, joining local events, or showing up for civic meetings. As your next Councilwoman, I will bring that same openness and commitment to City Hall.
With gratitude,
Ariana Martínez Lott

Issues & Priorities
# Where Drew stands.
Real priorities for real families. Here's what Drew is fighting for on the City Council.
## Public Safety
Drew's experience of over 40 years in law enforcement gives him the insight needed to understand the challenges our police and fire personnel face as they work to protect Clovis.
- Fully fund first responders
- Support neighborhood policing
- Invest in emergency preparedness
## Responsible Leadership
Local government should be transparent, accountable, and careful with taxpayer dollars. Drew believes that common sense governance is one of the reasons Clovis has been successful. While Drew will speak about national and state topics publicly, he will avoid bringing these issues into the Council Chambers whenever possible unless there is a direct link to a Clovis-specific issue. Our focus should be on public safety, good roads, clean parks and trails, and all the other things our citizens expect their local government to do. Sometimes, your Council will have to make decisions that you don't agree with. I understand that, and when I have to make a decision that is controversial I will explain why I am making that decision. You may end up a little mad at me but you will always understand why I felt the need to vote in the manner I did. That's an element in Lincoln's "public opinion bath." There may be times when Drew and the Council need to make unpopular decisions, possibly very unpopular decisions, but Drew will always explain why that decision needs to be made or not be made. There may be times, and there have been several over the last 9 years, when Drew was the 1-4 vote on an issue he believed in or seriously doubted and he could not vote in favor of. Abraham Lincoln called these moments "public opinion baths."
- Transparent budgets and clear priorities
- Fiscal responsibility, no waste
- Open communication with residents
## Local Businesses
Small businesses are the heart of our city. Having small businesses and larger ones we can get the mix of goods and services we all want. Drew will cut red tape whenever possible, recruit out of town businesses, and help entrepreneurs open, grow, and hire right here at home. Drew will support businesses, big and small, and work to make it easier for them to open and stay open. As Mayor during the first year of COVID, Drew worked hard to reopen Clovis and lobbied State officials, including the Governor, to ease the restrictions placed on small businesses while allowing big businesses to stay open. We need to advocate for and protect our local businesses from the long-arm of Sacramento that overlooks local small businesses and favors larger national businesses that donate large amounts to some State elected officials at the expense of local businesses and their local employees ... our neighbors!
## Community & Families
From parks to neighborhood events, Drew is committed to a city that brings people together and where families can put down roots for generations. That means working to strengthen our older neighborhoods so young families will be able to buy their first homes and grow with our community. We need to make “the Clovis Way of Life” affordable for our children and later generations too.
- Strengthen older neighborhoods
- Keep the Clovis Way of Life affordable
- Invest in youth programs
- Support seniors and veterans
## Quality of Life
Clean streets, well-kept parks and trails, and reliable services aren't extras — they're the foundation of a great city. Drew will push to add additional trails in our older neighborhoods in SW Clovis, and he understands that quality of life begins with a safe community.
- Well-kept parks and trails
- Additional trails in SW Clovis' older neighborhoods
- Cleaner, safer streets
- Reliable core city services
## Responsible Growth
Our city is growing — and growth must be planned, thoughtful, and true to who we are. District 5 will be the next growth area of Clovis. The “Heritage Grove” planned area will bring mixed types of housing, commercial growth, and trails and parks. We need to ensure we have planned and common-sense growth that strengthens neighborhoods, not overwhelms them.
- Planned, common-sense growth in District 5
- Support the Heritage Grove planned area
- Mixed housing, commercial, trails and parks
- Modernize infrastructure
Op-Ed
August 2026
## The 2017 Proposed Mental Health Hospital in the Dry Creek Business Park
Drew shares his full thought process on 2017's proposed acute-care mental health facility in Clovis — what he learned touring a similar UHS hospital in the Sacramento/Elk Grove area, his three unresolved concerns, and why he believes the need is real but this location was wrong. This is from the campaign trail in 2017, but is an example of how Drew analyzes the issues that are important.
Read the full op-ed
I have been asked in public forums, via email and Facebook, and while I'm out walking precincts about my opinion of the proposed mental health hospital at Clovis and Alluvial Avenues. I'm going to go into some detail, as this is not a simple "Yes or No" issue. Please bear with me.
As a law enforcement officer for over 40 years, I have significant history and knowledge on the issue of mentally ill persons. They come from all walks of life and backgrounds, and I have seen both personally and professionally the harm that untreated mental illness causes to the individual, their families, and sometimes to our society through acts of violence.
I also have a great deal of experience dealing with the homeless. While Clovis does not have a great deal of homeless persons, Fresno does and it bleeds over. As a Police Officer in Santa Barbara for 4 years (1980-1984) I had a significant amount of contact and dealings with violent, intoxicated and mentally ill homeless people on a daily basis most times.
It can be easy to dismiss this problem, until it ends up on your doorstep ... literally or figuratively. Being categorized as mentally ill or homeless comes with a societal stigma, and people with these issues need to be treated with respect, understanding and dignity.
I attended several Council meetings, and listened to the concerns of many, both pro and con, about this proposed facility. As I understand it, UHS has abandoned its project at the current location and is seeking another, more suitable, location. However, I think it's important for citizens to understand both my position and my thought process on this issue, as I live close to the proposed facility too. In fact, I may live too close to be permitted to cast a vote on this location due to the proposed site being within my statutory "conflict of interest" zone.
When I was the interim Chief of Police in Kingsburg, I dealt with a similar issue when a mental health corporation wanted to move into the vacant Kingsburg Hospital. We did our research, and the Police Department made several proposals that were incorporated into the eventual agreement. I attended several Planning Commission and City Council meetings and testified. I also addressed the concerns from some citizens and fielded their questions. The Kingsburg facility was a different kind of facility, it was a long-term care facility where a patient would stay for 3-9 months. It was approved and I spoke with the Kingsburg Chief (a friend) who said that the facility has been no problem at all.
This proposed facility is different. It is an acute care facility, where a patient in crisis comes either directly to the facility, or through an emergency room. The average stay is 7-9 days. They are then released when they are stabilized. I spoke with the representative for the developer, and he scheduled a visit to a similar UHS facility in Sacramento (right on 99 on the border of Elk Grove) and I took a day trip by myself to tour it.
The Sacramento facility looks similar to the care facility on Alluvial east of Willow. It appears to someone driving down the street as an office building or clinic, nothing that screams "mental hospital" or a correctional facility. This facility was built sometime in the late 1980's, and the neighboring area developed around it (not what we have proposed here.) It has controlled access and egress. The interior courtyards have "no climb" walls that would take Spiderman to get out of. It was clean, there were both medical and mental health professionals on staff, and it appeared to be well run. I spoke with the staff, and they answered my questions. I specifically asked about the release of homeless persons after treatment. UHS said that they are never released out the front door, they make arrangements for a bed in a shelter and drive them there. When I left, I considered having this specific type of facility in our city, and here were my concerns:
1. When dealing with a homeless person, can they make arrangements for them to go directly (voluntarily) to drug or alcohol treatment? Many homeless are what are referred to as "dual diagnosis" patients, mental health and addiction issues. If both aren't treated successfully, it causes a roller coaster effect which pushes them back into a mental health crisis cycle. Once the patient is stabilized mentally, they would be much more amenable to getting the next level of treatment. This seems to be the most holistic approach to resolve the problem.
2. Transporting the homeless to shelters in Sacramento is fine, but Fresno does not have sufficient shelters or "beds" for the homeless. (This is obviously a whole other issue.) In the event that a homeless person declines further treatment and refuses to go to a shelter, what then? Nothing keeps them from leaving the facility, after treatment, and making Clovis their new home, so to speak. This is a major concern for many citizens, including myself.
3. Would UHS consider making this an adolescent-only facility? Mental health issues affect our young, and we see that with the rise in teen suicide locally. Since teens would have a home to return to, we don't have to deal with the homeless issue. Suicide is the second leading cause of death for high school age youth. With the recent teen suicides in Clovis schools, having a local acute care facility with available bed space would be an imperative.
We absolutely need local mental health treatment facilities, and I think that Clovis needs to be part of the regional solution. We should not say "Isn't there a place in Fresno for this?" because, frankly, that's not fair. We are a city of almost 110,000, we need to be a major player in resolving all of our region's problems.
The lack of mental health "beds" is also one of the reasons that people have to wait in emergency rooms so long: the hospitals cannot by law transfer the mentally ill person to a "lesser care" facility, they have to wait for a "bed" to transfer them to. Thus, the bottle neck.
As with most real estate and planning issues, it's about the location. The proposed site is not the right location in my opinion. If another location was found, I would give it serious consideration but also listen to the concerns of our citizens.
There is a definite need for this type of facility because there are citizens in desperate need of care. We need to temper our concerns about this type of facility in our city with the need for compassion for the mentally ill and their families.
As your Councilmember, I will do the "homework" necessary on the important issues that affect our community. I have no problem getting in my car to go look at an issue because I'm a more visual learner, and some things cannot be properly described. There may come a time when my "Yes" or "No" may not be popular with everyone, that's the nature of governing. All I can promise is that I will make the best choice using thought and research.

Bringing Proven Leadership and Results to Fresno County
## A Vision for
Excellence in Education
As a dedicated advocate for education and a leader with a proven track record, I am honored to announce my candidacy for Fresno County Superintendent of Schools. This is not just a campaign—it’s a commitment to ensuring every child, educator, and family in our community thrives through accessible, high-quality education.
​
When we speak about RESULTS, we are
aiming for higher educational outcomes
for our students.
## Proven Leadership
You Can Trust
Throughout my career, I have consistently delivered impactful results. From driving innovative programs to improving student outcomes, my leadership has been rooted in collaboration, accountability, and a deep understanding of the diverse needs of our community. My experience has taught me that successful schools are built on strong partnerships—between educators, families, and local stakeholders.
## Results That Matter
As a collaborative leader, whether as a school site leader or as a District Superintendent, I fostered a culture of teamwork and trust that encouraged employees to hold themselves accountable for providing exceptional service to the students in their care. This shared sense of responsibility not only strengthened our collective mission but also empowered every individual to contribute meaningfully to the success of our schools and the well-being of our community.
​
Click below to view some of the most significant results accomplished by my teams under my leadership. Together, we:
Learn More
As your next Superintendent
of Schools, I intend to prioritize the following 3 GOALS:
Goals
## GOAL #1: 3rd Grade Literacy
FACT: In Fresno County, 60% of third graders on average are not meeting reading standards. That means that in a class of 25 students, 15 are not meeting literacy standards.
​
​
​​
​
Why Reading Matters
Reading is not merely a skill—it is the foundation upon which all other academic competencies are built, including mathematical reasoning, scientific inquiry, and critical thinking. By empowering students to have strong literacy skills from an early age, we will pave the way for success in every academic discipline and prepare them to navigate the complexities of the modern world.
​
How reading confidence affects our students
A focus on reading will not only elevate our county’s literacy rates but it will also allow us to tackle a variety of interconnected challenges faced by students.
When our children acquire strong reading skills, it will nurture their self-esteem and confidence, providing them with the tools to express themselves effectively and navigate their academic journeys with assurance.
Furthermore, by improving literacy, we can alleviate anxiety and frustration often stemming from academic struggles, fostering a more positive school environment.
Equipped with better reading proficiency, our students will more likely engage in classroom activities, exhibit better behavior, and form stronger connections with peers and teachers.
My response
As part of my educational agenda, I will develop a comprehensive multi-year literacy plan in collaboration with our educational team to address this priority effectively. I am witnessing an exciting return to the “Back to Basics” science of reading approach that I successfully used for twenty years in my own classrooms. I hope to champion this and other proven methods in the development of our county's plan to achieve significant results for the students in our schools.
​
With this plan, we will be taking a foundational step toward enabling Fresno County’s youth to flourish both academically and personally.
## GOAL #2: Partner with Parents
and Families!
Why is this important in education?
Parents play an essential role as the first and primary educators in their children's critical early years. As a parent myself, I appreciated having access to information that helped me support my children at school. At the same time, as a teacher and administrator, I saw the impact of strong school to home relationships. In short, our students achieve higher outcomes when they are supported by school and family communities sharing a common vision.
What I know works…
Providing parents with the necessary support and knowledge around early childhood educational milestones
Engaging parents in opportunities to learn how to help their children navigate social, emotional and academic challenges as they matriculate through the system
Partnering with local parenting groups such as Fresno State's Parent University to create modules focused on topics of interest
Fostering relationships with local community groups to help support family to school connections
​
What’s my plan?
I aim to collaborate with District leaders and community organizations specializing in parent engagement programs to help parents actively engage in their children's education. ​
​
If we partner with parents and families to support their children, we will be able to strengthen the bridge between home and school, ensuring a more cohesive and collaborative approach to education.
## GOAL #3: Let's Increase our Return
on Investment in Education
What I know…
Fresno County receives significant federal and state dollars for TK-12 education totaling in the billions. Yet, our students continue to struggle, with 56% not meeting standards in English Language Arts and 68% not meeting standards in Math in 2023-24.
Why is this?
Simply put, our current approach isn’t working. My experiences in both Clovis and Central Unified have taught me that we must have the courage to change course when our students are not achieving the results they deserve.
​
The answer?
There are teachers all over our county whose students are achieving great results! We need to work together to collaborate on systems and programs that are yielding positive outcomes on a consistent basis. Only through listening to each other, supporting our teachers, and identifying the most effective programs and methodologies, will we begin to move the needle on student achievement.
​
Therefore in Fresno County, I aim to work alongside districts to explore proven approaches so that our significant investment in education returns the results we all need for our kids.
## My Pledge to
Fresno County
The Office of the Fresno County Superintendent of Schools
Leadership and Support for
Educational Excellence
As your next Superintendent of Schools, I would not be “the boss of” the 31 School District Superintendents. Each elected School Board independently collaborates with their own district on their unique vision. However, I will be the “Listener-in-Chief,” the “Supporter-in-Chief,” and most of all the “Inspirer-in-Chief” for the entire county. Together we can accomplish significant results for the students of Fresno County, where my role is to champion and unify our District Superintendents into a larger countywide vision of success.
​
I believe that I have the drive, the passion, the experience, and most of all the capacity to build meaningful relationships to achieve the results our kids desperately need.
​
As your next Superintendent of Schools, I will be engaged in the following RESPONSIBILITIES:
Learn More
## Collaborative Leadership for Transformative Change
Imagine a future where every school district in Fresno County operates with systems designed to maximize efficiency and effectiveness.
​
Collaboration is key to achieving our vision. I aim to work hand-in-hand with educators, parents, and community stakeholders to build systems that empower both students and teachers. By leveraging the lessons learned in Clovis and Central, we can pioneer solutions that uplift every district in the county. Whether it’s tapping into community support, optimizing resources, or fostering innovation, my approach is rooted in practical, results-oriented leadership that makes a difference where it matters most—in the classroom.
## Join Me in Shaping
the Future
Education is the cornerstone of a thriving community, and Fresno County deserves a Superintendent who leads with integrity, vision, and results. Together, we can empower our schools to be models of excellence and innovation.
​
I invite you to join me on this journey. Let’s shape a brighter future for our children and our county. Together, we can achieve extraordinary things.
## Your support matters
Vote for proven leadership.
Vote for proven results.
Vote for a brighter tomorrow.
